tip: For a stretch of time, Swedish uses 'i': 'duschar i tio minuter' = showers for ten minutes.
'Man' is the general you or one: 'man får bada' = you may swim. It always takes a singular verb, 'får'.
Swedish often states the posture of things: a cat placed there 'sitter' (sits) rather than just is, as in 'en katt sitter i fönstret'.
'Kommer att' marks the future: 'kommer att vara' = will be. The negation slots in between: 'kommer inte att vara sena'.
Some commands include 'dig' (yourself): 'sätt dig' = sit down, 'skynda dig' = hurry up.
'I och för sig' = in itself / admittedly – a very common hedging phrase.
'Visste' is the irregular past of 'veta' (to know): 'jag visste inte' = I didn't know. No '-de' ending is added.
Inside an 'att' clause, 'inte' comes before the verb: 'att han inte bor här'. In a main clause it would be 'han bor inte'.
When 'vad' is the subject of the next clause, Swedish adds 'som': 'vad som händer' = what happens. The 'som' cannot be dropped.
Begin with an 'eftersom' (since) clause and the main verb still comes second, ahead of the subject: 'stannade vi hemma'.
Swedes often say 'det ordnar sig' to express calm optimism about the future.
'Sig' is the self word for he, she, and they: 'hon sminkar sig' = she puts makeup on herself.
For body parts Swedish usually uses the definite form, not a possessive: 'ansiktet' (the face) means my face when the owner is obvious.
'Vaknar' (wake up) takes no self word in Swedish: 'jag vaknar', not 'jag vaknar mig'.
'Kanske' can pull the verb forward: 'kanske kommer han' = maybe he comes, with the verb before the subject.
Swedish says 'i telefon' (in the phone) for on the phone, using 'i' where English uses on.
'Lära sig' means to learn; 'lära' without 'sig' means to teach. Here 'lärt sig' marks learning, not teaching.
Use 'mitt' (not 'min') before an 'ett' word: 'fel' is one, so it is 'mitt fel', my fault.
To want a thing, Swedish uses 'vill ha' (want to have), not 'vill' alone: 'vill inte ha något' = don't want anything.
'Sina' means one's own and points back to the subject: 'sina ögon' are his own eyes, not someone else's.
'Tycka om' means to like, and it splits: 'inte' lands between the two parts, 'tyckte inte om'.
'Inte heller' means not either: 'inte heller jag' = me neither.
'Inte alls' = not at all – a common way to strengthen a negation.
'Inte bestämt sig än' = not decided yet: 'än' (yet) sits at the end of a negative sentence.
In an 'om' (if) clause, 'inte' comes before the verb: 'om du inte vill', not 'om du vill inte'.
Start with a time phrase and the verb still comes second: 'nästa vecka börjar' puts 'börjar' before the subject.
'På landet' means in the countryside, not on the land; 'landet' here is rural areas, not a nation.
'Varandra' means each other: 'känt varandra' = have known each other.
After 'som', a profession normally takes no article: 'jobbat som läkare' = worked as a doctor, no a.
Daily routine verbs often take a self word: 'kammar mig' (comb myself), 'klär mig' (dress myself).
